scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Several users report intermittent slowness and claim
"router0 is dropping our packets" -- they think router0 is silently discarding
traffic it should forward (a forwarding/ACL problem or an overloaded box) and want
it restarted. Please confirm that router0 is dropping traffic and tell us the fix.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The network is healthy. Router0 is not dropping, discarding, or rate-limiting
any traffic, and there is no forwarding or ACL fault anywhere in the topology.

A thorough inspection of every plausible failure mechanism on router0 found
nothing wrong:

• iptables (filter, nat, mangle): all chains carry the default ACCEPT policy;
  no DROP or REJECT rule exists anywhere in the table.
• ip_forward: set to 1 — kernel forwarding is enabled.
• tc qdiscs: standard fq_codel on all three interfaces with no netem loss/
  delay injected and no bandwidth policers attached.
• Interface counters (eth0/eth1/eth2): RX dropped = 0, TX dropped = 0,
  errors = 0, missed = 0, carrier = 0, collisions = 0 across all interfaces
  after sustained cross-topology traffic.
• Routing table: all eight subnets present and correctly installed in the FIB
  (three directly connected, five via RIP from router1/router2).
• RIP convergence: all three routers show fully converged tables with fresh
  route timers (~3 min); no missing prefixes, no routing loops.

End-to-end data-plane tests confirmed full bidirectional reachability with 0%
packet loss across every measured path: IT LAN ↔ Servers, IT LAN ↔ Internet,
CS LAN ↔ Internet, CS LAN ↔ Office, Principle LAN ↔ IT LAN, and
Principle LAN ↔ Servers — all traversing router0.

Root cause: there is no fault; the users' premise ("router0 is dropping our
packets") is incorrect. The "intermittent slowness" is unrelated to any
forwarding or ACL problem on router0.

Corrective action: no configuration change or restart is needed — and
restarting router0 would actually be harmful, as it would tear down the RIP
session with router1 and black-hole traffic for the 30–180 seconds it takes
RIP to reconverge. The helpdesk ticket should be closed as a false alarm, and
users should be asked to provide specific packet-capture evidence if the
perceived slowness persists.

The inferences follow logically from the observations and the investigation covers the essential checks needed to rule out router0 as the cause.
